Let  

P(x)= (1+x)^{10000}= Σ_{k=0}^{10000} C(10000,k) x^{k} .

Write every exponent modulo 502.  
If we reduce P(x) modulo x^{502}-1 we get a polynomial of degree ≤ 501

R(x)= Σ_{r=0}^{501} S_r x^{r}            (1)

whose coefficient of x^{r} is exactly S_r.  
To know S_r (mod 503) it is therefore enough to determine R(x) (mod 503).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Behaviour of (1+x)^{502}  (mod 503)

Because 503 is prime,

C(502,k)= (502·501·…·(502-k+1))/k! ≡ (−1)^k   (mod 503)

so, in F₅₀₃[x],

(1+x)^{502}= Σ_{k=0}^{502} (−1)^k x^{k}= Σ_{k=0}^{502} (−x)^k.   (2)

For any element z∈F₅₀₃ with z≠−1 and z^{502}=1 (i.e. for every 502-nd root of unity except −1),

(1+z)^{502}= Σ_{k=0}^{502} (−z)^k
            = (1−(−z)^{503})/(1+z)
            = (1+z)/(1+z)=1.   (3)

For z=−1, clearly (1+z)^{502}=0.

Thus, for every 502-nd root of unity ω different from −1 we have

(1+ω)^{502}=1,       (1+ω)^{10000}= (1+ω)^{19·502+462}= (1+ω)^{462}.   (4)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Evaluation of P(x) at the 502 roots of unity

Let the 502 roots of x^{502}−1 in F₅₀₃ be ω^0,ω^1,…,ω^{501}, with ω a primitive root.  
From (4):

P(ω^j)= (1+ω^j)^{10000}=  
        0              if   ω^j=−1  (j=251),  
        (1+ω^j)^{462}   otherwise.                              (5)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Identifying R(x)

The remainder R(x) in (1) is the unique polynomial of degree ≤ 501 that equals P(x) at all 502 roots of unity.  
The polynomial (1+x)^{462} already has degree 462≤501 and, by (5), coincides with P(x) at every root (including −1, where both equal 0).  
Hence

R(x) ≡ (1+x)^{462}         (mod 503, x^{502}−1).                  (6)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Coefficients modulo 503

From (6) and (1):

For 0 ≤ r ≤ 462      S_r ≡ C(462,r)   (mod 503),  
For 463 ≤ r ≤ 501    S_r ≡ 0          (mod 503).                  (7)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Which C(462,r) are multiples of 503?

Because 0<462<503, neither 462! nor any k! (k≤462) contains the prime 503 in its factorisation.  
Thus 503 cannot divide C(462,r) for any r (0≤r≤462).  
Consequently the only S_r that are divisible by 503 are those with r ≥ 463.

There are 501−463+1 = 39 such indices.

Exactly 39 of the numbers S₀,S₁,…,S₅₀₁ are multiples of 503.

\boxed{39}

Step 1.  Express S₍ᵣ₎ as a coefficient.  
Write  
 F(x) = (1+x)^{10000} = Σ_{k=0}^{10000} {10000 \choose k} x^{k}.  
Reducing exponents modulo 502, the remainder of F(x) upon division by x^{502}-1 is

 F₀(x) = Σ_{r=0}^{501} S_r x^{r}.                                        (1)

So S_r is the coefficient of x^{r} in F₀(x).

Step 2.  Work modulo the prime 503.  
Throughout this step all equalities are in the ring  
 R = 𝔽_{503}[x]/(x^{502}-1).

Step 3.  A key fact about (1+x)^{502}.  
Because 503 is prime, Fermat’s little theorem gives (1+u)^{503} ≡ 1+u^{503} (mod 503) for every u.  
Let u be any 502-nd root of unity (u^{502}=1).  Then u^{503}=u, so

 (1+u)^{503} ≡ 1+u.                                                (2)

If 1+u≠0 (i.e. u≠−1), divide (2) by 1+u to obtain (1+u)^{502}=1.  
If u=−1, then (1+u)=0 and (2) is still true.  Hence for every 502-nd root of unity u,

 (1+u)^{502}= { 1  if u≠−1
                 0  if u=−1 }.

Consequently, in the ring R we have

 (1+x)^{502} ≡ 1         (mod x+1).                               (3)

Step 4.  Reduce the exponent 10000.  
Write 10000 = 502·19 + 462.  Using (3),

 (1+x)^{10000} = (1+x)^{502·19} · (1+x)^{462}
                ≡ 1^{19} · (1+x)^{462}
                ≡ (1+x)^{462}                        in R.        (4)

Step 5.  Identify the coefficients S_r (mod 503).  
Because degrees ≤461 remain unchanged and every term of degree ≥463 disappears in R,

 F₀(x) ≡ (1+x)^{462}
        = Σ_{r=0}^{462} {462 \choose r} x^{r}.                    (5)

Comparing (1) and (5) we obtain, modulo 503,

 S_r ≡ { {462 \choose r}  for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462
          0                for 463 ≤ r ≤ 501 }.                   (6)

Step 6.  Determine which S_r are multiples of 503.  
Since 0 ≤ 462 < 503, the binomial coefficients {462 \choose r} are all non-zero mod 503; none of the first 463 sums is divisible by 503.

For 463 ≤ r ≤ 501 the congruence (6) gives S_r ≡ 0 (mod 503), so each of these 39 sums is a multiple of 503.

Step 7.  Count them.  
There are 501 − 463 + 1 = 39 residue classes with r > 462.

Therefore, exactly 39 of the numbers S₀, S₁, …, S_{501} are divisible by the prime 503.

Step 1.  Write 10000 in base 503.  
   10000 = 19·503 + 443, so  
   n0 = 443 ,  n1 = 19.

Step 2.  Lucas’ Theorem (mod prime 503).  
For every k let k = k1·503 + k0 with 0 ≤ k0 ≤ 502 and 0 ≤ k1 ≤ 19.  
Then  
  \displaystyle\binom{10000}{k} ≡ \binom{19}{k_1}\binom{443}{k_0}  (mod 503),  
and the right–hand side is 0 whenever k0 > 443 (since that binomial coefficient is 0).

Step 3.  Express the congruence class of k (mod 502).  
Because 503 ≡ 1 (mod 502),  
  k = 503k1 + k0 ≡ k1 + k0  (mod 502).

With k1 ≤ 19 and k0 ≤ 443, the sum s = k1 + k0 satisfies 0 ≤ s ≤ 462.

Consequently
• if r ∈ {463, 464, … , 501} there is no k with k ≡ r (mod 502) for which  
  \binom{10000}{k} is non–zero; hence S_r = 0.

Step 4.  Evaluate S_r for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462.  
Here k1 + k0 = r, so

   S_r = Σ_{k1=0}^{19}  \binom{19}{k1}\binom{443}{r-k1}
       = coefficient of x^r in (1+x)^{19}(1+x)^{443}
       = coefficient of x^r in (1+x)^{462}
       = \binom{462}{r}.

Step 5.  Divisibility by 503.  
Because 503 > 462, every factorial in the expression of \binom{462}{r} is a product of numbers
strictly less than 503; hence 503 cannot divide any \binom{462}{r}.  
Thus

   S_r ≡ 0 (mod 503)  ⇔  r ∈ {463, 464, … , 501}.

There are 501 – 463 + 1 = 39 such residues.

Therefore, among S_0, S_1, … , S_{501} exactly 39 of them are multiples of 503.

Write each k (0 ≤ k ≤ 10000) in base 503:

k = 503 b + a , 0 ≤ a < 503 , 0 ≤ b ≤ 19 , a ≤ 443     (because 10000 = 19·503 + 443).

By Lucas’ theorem (mod 503):

C(10000, k) ≡ C(443, a) · C(19, b)   (mod 503). (1)

For a fixed residue r (0 ≤ r < 502),

k ≡ r  (mod 502) ⇔ 503 b + a ≡ r  (mod 502).

Since 503 ≡ 1 (mod 502), this is

a + b = r. (2)        (0 ≤ a ≤ 443 , 0 ≤ b ≤ 19).

But a + b never exceeds 443 + 19 = 462, so (2) can hold only when 0 ≤ r ≤ 462; for 463 ≤ r ≤ 501 no k satisfies the congruence.

Thus, for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462,

S_r = Σ_{a+b=r} C(443, a) C(19, b),

and for 463 ≤ r ≤ 501,

S_r = 0.                                                   (3)

The sum in (3) is exactly the coefficient of x^r in

(1+x)^{443} (1+x)^{19} = (1+x)^{462}.

Hence, for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462

S_r = C(462, r).                                           (4)

Now count how many S_r are divisible by the prime 503.

•  For 463 ≤ r ≤ 501 (total 39 values) we have S_r = 0, which is a multiple of 503.

•  For 0 ≤ r ≤ 462, note that 462 < 503.  When n < p (p prime), no interior binomial coefficient C(n,k) with 0 < k < n is divisible by p, because the factorials involve no multiples of p.  Consequently every C(462,r) (including the endpoints r = 0, 462) is non-zero modulo 503, so none of them is divisible by 503.

Therefore the only multiples of 503 among the 502 numbers S_0, S_1, …, S_{501} are the 39 zeros listed above.

Let p = 503 (a prime) and q = 502 = p – 1.

1.  Grouping the coefficients  
   For 0 ≤ r ≤ 501 let  

      S_r = Σ_{m≥0} C(10000 , qm + r),

   i.e. the sum of the binomial coefficients in row 10000 whose indices are ≡ r (mod q).

2.  Roots-of-unity filter  
   Over the field 𝔽_p choose g to be a generator of the multiplicative group (so g has order q).  
   Put ω = g.  Then

      S_r = (1/q) Σ_{j=0}^{q-1} ω^{-jr}(1+ω^j)^{10000}               (1)

   because 1/q ≡ –1 (mod p).

3.  Reducing the exponent 10000  
   In 𝔽_p each non-zero element a satisfies a^{p-1}=1.  
   For j ≠ 251 we have 1+ω^j ≠ 0, so

      (1+ω^j)^{10000} = (1+ω^j)^{10000 mod (p-1)} = (1+ω^j)^{462},

   since 10000 ≡ 462 (mod 502).  
   For j = 251 we have 1+ω^{251}=0, so the term vanishes.

4.  Converting the DFT sum to a coefficient problem  
   Let

      P(x) = (1+x)^{10000} = Σ_{k=0}^{10000} C(10000,k)x^k.

   Working in the quotient ring 𝔽_p[x]/(x^{502}–1) the condition x^{502}=1 sends every
   exponent k to k mod 502.  Hence the coefficient of x^r in P(x) mod (x^{502}–1) is exactly S_r (mod p).

   But in 𝔽_p,

      (1+x)^{503} ≡ 1 + x^{503} ≡ 1 + x      (mod p, x^{502}=1),

   so

      (1+x)^{10000} = (1+x)^{503·19+443}
                   ≡ [(1+x)^{503}]^{19}(1+x)^{443}
                   ≡ (1+x)^{19}(1+x)^{443}
                   = (1+x)^{462}              (mod p, x^{502}=1).

   Therefore, in that quotient ring,

      P(x) ≡ (1+x)^{462}.

5.  Reading off the S_r (mod 503)  
   (1+x)^{462} has degree 462.  Hence

      S_r ≡ C(462,r)  for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462,  
      S_r ≡ 0         for 463 ≤ r ≤ 501.               (2)

6.  Which C(462,r) are multiples of 503?  
   Because 462 < 503, the factorial 462! is invertible mod 503, so for 0 ≤ r ≤ 462

      C(462,r) ≠ 0  (mod 503).

   Thus none of the first 463 values S_r are divisible by 503.

7.  Counting the zeroes  
   From (2) every S_r with 463 ≤ r ≤ 501 is 0 mod 503.  There are

      501 – 463 + 1 = 39

   such indices.

Hence 39 of the numbers S_0, S_1, … , S_501 are divisible by 503.

Reduce all polynomials in 𝔽_{p}[ω] modulo ω^{p-1}-1; that makes ω^{p-1}=1, hence ω^{kp+r}=ω^{r}.

1.  The generating-function point of view  
   Put  
      F(ω)= (1+ω)^{10000}= Σ_{k=0}^{10000} {10000 \choose k} ω^{k}.  
   After reducing modulo ω^{502}-1 (and still over the integers) every exponent k is
   replaced by its remainder mod 502, so the coefficient of ω^{r}(0≤r≤501) becomes exactly  
      S_{r}= Σ_{m≥0}{10000 \choose 502m+r}.  
   In other words, in the ring ℤ[ω]/(ω^{502}-1) the polynomial whose coefficients are the S_{r}’s is simply the reduction of (1+ω)^{10000}.

2.  Working modulo the prime 503  
   We now work in 𝔽_{503}[ω]/(ω^{502}-1).  
   Fermat gives (1+ω)^{503}≡1+ω^{503} (mod 503).  
   But in our ring ω^{503}=ω·ω^{502}=ω, hence  
      (1+ω)^{503}≡1+ω  (mod 503, ω^{502}-1).  
   Therefore for any non-negative integer k,
      (1+ω)^{503k}≡(1+ω)^{k}.  

3.  Reduce the exponent 10000  
   Write 10000 = 503·19 + 443.  
   Then  
      (1+ω)^{10000} = (1+ω)^{503·19}(1+ω)^{443}  
                    ≡ (1+ω)^{19}(1+ω)^{443}  
                    =  (1+ω)^{462}           (mod 503, ω^{502}-1).  

   The exponent 462 is already <502, so no further reduction on exponents is needed.

4.  Reading off the coefficients  
   Hence, for 0 ≤ r ≤ 501,  
      S_{r} ≡ coefficient of ω^{r} in (1+ω)^{462}  (mod 503).  

   • For 0 ≤ r ≤ 462 that coefficient is the ordinary binomial number {462 \choose r}.  
     Because 462 < 503, the numerator 462! contains no factor 503, so
     {462 \choose r} is not divisible by 503 for any r.  
     Thus S_{r} ≢ 0 (mod 503) for r ≤ 462.

   • For 463 ≤ r ≤ 501 the coefficient of ω^{r} in (1+ω)^{462} is 0, so S_{r} ≡ 0 (mod 503).  
     Hence every such S_{r} is a multiple of 503.

5.  Counting  
   The indices r with 463 ≤ r ≤ 501 inclusive amount to  
      501 − 463 + 1 = 39.

Therefore 39 of the numbers S₀, S₁, …, S₅₀₁ are divisible by the prime 503.

Step 1.  Express S₍ᵣ₎ as a coefficient.  
Write  

  (1+x)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ = ∑_{k=0}^{10000} {10000\choose k} x^{k}.  

Reducing exponents modulo 502 folds together all terms whose exponents are congruent mod 502:  

  (1+x)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ ≡ ∑_{r=0}^{501} S_r x^{r}  (mod x^{502}-1). (1)

Thus, for every r, S_r is the coefficient of x^{r} in the polynomial (1+x)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ taken modulo x^{502}-1.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 2.  Work modulo the prime 503 (note that 502 = 503 − 1).  

Because 503 is prime, for any a,b we have the “Freshman’s dream’’  

  (a+b)^{503} ≡ a^{503}+b^{503} (mod 503).

Write 10000 = 19·503 + 443, so  

  (1+x)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ = ((1+x)^{503})^{19}(1+x)^{443}.  

Modulo 503,  

  (1+x)^{503} ≡ 1 + x^{503}.  

Hence  

  (1+x)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ ≡ (1 + x^{503})^{19}(1+x)^{443} (mod 503). (2)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 3.  Also reduce exponents modulo 502.  

Because x^{502} ≡ 1 (mod x^{502}-1), we have x^{503} ≡ x.  
Therefore, modulo 503 ​and​ modulo x^{502}-1,

  (1 + x^{503})^{19} ≡ (1 + x)^{19}.  

Combine with (2):

  (1+x)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ ≡ (1+x)^{19}(1+x)^{443} = (1+x)^{462}  
              (mod 503 , x^{502}-1). (3)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 4.  Read off S_r modulo 503.  

The right-hand side of (3) has degree 462, so

  For 0 ≤ r ≤ 462 : S_r ≡ {462\choose r} (mod 503)  
  For 463 ≤ r ≤ 501 : S_r ≡ 0      (mod 503). (4)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 5.  Decide when 503 divides S_r.  

Since 503 > 462, the prime 503 does not divide 462!, so it cannot divide any binomial coefficient {462\choose r}.  
Thus by (4)

  •  For r = 0,1,2,…,462  S_r is ​not​ divisible by 503.  
  •  For r = 463,464,…,501 S_r ​is​ divisible by 503.

The number of r in the latter range is

  501 − 463 + 1 = 39.

\]

\sum |\,\text{diagonal}\,|^{2}=800\)

\[

------------------------------------------------

\[

\[

\;\Longrightarrow\;

Step 1.  Components and how the number of cousins is obtained  

Write S as the disjoint union of its connected components, where two elements of S are put in the same component when every consecutive gap between them is at most 2.  
Inside one component list its elements in increasing order  

x1 < x2 < … < xm                (m = size of the component).

For every xi we must choose the partner  
        xi – 1  (call the choice L)  or  xi + 1  (call the choice R)

subject to

a) if xi+1 = xi + 1 (two consecutive elements) then xi must be paired to the left (L) and xi+1 must be paired to the right (R);

b) if xi+1 = xi + 2 then the orientation RL is forbidden (they may not both use the number xi + 1).

No other restrictions exist and, once the orientations are fixed, the partner set T is fixed as well.  
Consequently the number of admissible orientation strings is exactly the number of cousin sets that the component produces; the total number of cousins of S is the product of these numbers over all components.

Step 2.  An upper bound for one component  

Inside a component let us look at all possible orientation strings of length m which avoid the forbidden pattern RL between two elements that are 2 apart.  
Among all components of size m the “loosest’’ one is the even–number chain  

{a, a+2, a+4, …, a+2(m–1)};           for it the only restriction is “no RL”.

For this particular chain the number of allowed strings is easily counted:

let A(m) be that number,  
let Fm(L)  (resp. Fm(R) ) be the number of strings of length m ending in L (resp. R).

Recurrence  
Fm(L) = Fm–1(L)                    (because a final L cannot follow an R)  
Fm(R) = Fm–1(L)+Fm–1(R) = A(m–1).

With F1(L)=F1(R)=1 one gets

A(1)=2, A(2)=3, A(3)=4, … , A(m)=m+1.

Adding further constraints (having two consecutive elements, extra pairs at distance 2, …) can only decrease the count, hence

Lemma.  Every connected component with m elements contributes at most m+1 cousins, and equality is attained only by the even–number chain described above.

Step 3.  Necessity of a very large component  

4040 = 2^3 · 5 · 101 contains the prime 101.  
Because 101 is itself larger than m+1 whenever m < 100, the lemma forces every set S with 4040 cousins to contain a connected component of size at least 100.  
(Indeed, one needs m+1 = 101, hence m = 100.)

So |S| ≥ 100, and we still have to provide the remaining factor 40 = 2^3 · 5.

Step 4.  Producing the factor 40 with as few extra elements as possible  

• A single element (a singleton component) supplies the factor 2.  
• The smallest way to obtain the factor 5 is a 4-element even chain, whose contribution is 5.  
Therefore

40 = 5 · 2 · 2 · 2

can be produced with

4 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 7 additional elements,

and 7 is minimal: every component giving a factor c≥2 needs at least c–1 elements, so any decomposition of 40 different from 5·2·2·2 would need at least  
(4)+(1)+(1)+(1)=7 elements as well, and none can do it with 6 or fewer.

Step 5.  A concrete set S with 4040 cousins and 107 elements  

Take

A = {0,2,4,…,198}                            (100 elements, contributes 101)  
B = {300,302,304,306}                        (4-element chain, contributes 5)  
C1 = {400},    C2 = {410},    C3 = {420}     (three singletons, each contributes 2)

The gaps between different components are at least 3, hence they are independent.  
The total number of cousins is

101 × 5 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 4040,

and the total size is

100 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 107.

Step 6.  Minimality of 107  

• At least 100 elements are compulsory (Step 3).  
• To supply the remaining factor 40 one needs at least 7 more elements (Step 4).

Therefore every set with exactly 4040 cousins contains at least 107 elements, and the construction above shows that 107 can indeed be reached.
